title: Why Staying Late After School Is A Mistake
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that staying late at school, whether out of pride, guilt, or overwhelm, ultimately makes teachers worse at their jobs rather than better. He contends that effectiveness in the classroom depends on being rested, clear-eyed, and patient each morning, and that chronic overwork erodes those qualities even when teachers insist they can handle it. The article challenges the assumption that more preparation time produces better lessons, invoking Parkinson's Law to explain why work expands to fill the time allotted and why a shorter, focused deadline sharpens both concentration and the final product. Linsin also faults inefficient planning habits — distraction, excessive socializing with colleagues, and directionless lesson design — as bigger culprits than insufficient hours. He recommends choosing one clear objective per lesson, setting a firm early departure deadline, and leaving promptly without lingering. The piece closes with an appeal to protect personal time for family, exercise, and rest as a direct investment in teaching quality.
points: Long hours after school do not make a teacher more effective; they erode the rest and clarity needed to teach well the next day.
Parkinson's Law explains why open-ended prep time gets wasted — work expands to fill whatever time is allotted.
Giving yourself less time to plan increases focus and reduces the chance for distraction, uncertainty, and inefficiency.
Most wasted prep time comes from inefficient habits — chatting with colleagues, indecision, and lack of a clear lesson objective — not too few hours.
Choose one clear objective per lesson and the simplest direct path to it, then set a firm, earlier deadline and stick to it.
quotes: It makes them feel as if they’re doing everything they can for their students.
Because staying late after school doesn’t make you a better teacher. It makes you worse.
You need to be rested and refreshed before greeting your students each morning. You need to be clear-eyed and quick thinking, patient and observant.
Parkinson’s Law is the tendency to expand a task in complexity and importance in relation to the time given for its completion.
The law also states that when you give yourself less time you become more focused. Your concentration increases.
They end up with lessons that are bloated and directionless and that students struggle to understand.
Set a deadline, say half or two-thirds the amount of time you usually stay after school, then stick with it. Turn out the lights. Close the door. Walk swiftly to your car without looking back.
